1.note: The words **Pashhur** and **Immer** are the names of men.

Jeremiah is providing background information to help readers understand what happens next in the story. In your translation, introduce this information in a way that would be natural in your own language and culture.
See how you translated this phrase in 17:26. This also occurs in verse 2.

The implication is that **these words** are the prophecy that Jeremiah had just spoken, which the previous chapter records. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [these words of judgment that he had just spoken]

2.note: The implication is that Pashhur, who was the chief officer of the temple, had Jeremiah beaten or flogged rather than that he himself **struck** him only once. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [And Pashhur had Jeremiah the prophet beaten]

The **stocks** were a kind of wooden frame that held a prisoner’s feet, hands, and neck in place so that he could not move. If your readers would not be familiar with what stocks are, you could use the name of a similar thing that your readers would recognize, or you could use a more general term. Alternate translation: [in wooden restraints]

3.q: לֹ֤א פַשְׁחוּר֙ קָרָ֤א יְהוָה֙ שְׁמֶ֔⁠ךָ כִּ֖י אִם מָג֥וֹר מִ⁠סָּבִֽיב
3.note: The implication is that Yahweh is giving Pashhur a new name in order to announce what is going to happen to him. In this culture, a name could describe what a person was like or what would happen to him. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [Yahweh is giving you a new name that shows what will happen to you: he is no longer calling you Pashhur, but rather Magor-Missabib, which means “Terror on Every Side”]
See how you translated the similar expression in 6:25. This also occurs in verse 10.

3.q: לֹ֤א פַשְׁחוּר֙ & קָרָ֤א יְהוָה֙ שְׁמֶ֔⁠ךָ כִּ֖י אִם־מָג֥וֹר מִ⁠סָּבִֽיב
3.note: Jeremiah is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. He means that Yahweh will now call Pashhur’s name Magor-Missabib. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [Yahweh has not called your name Pashhur, but rather, he has called it Magor-Missabib]

4.note: See how you translated the similar expression in 2:5.

4.q: הִנְ⁠נִי֩ נֹתֶנְ⁠ךָ֨ לְ⁠מָג֜וֹר לְ⁠ךָ֣ וּ⁠לְ⁠כָל אֹהֲבֶ֗י⁠ךָ
4.note: If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate this so that there is not a quotation within a quotation. Alternate translation: [Yahweh is making you a terror to yourself and to all your lovers]

Yahweh is using **Behold me making you** as a common expression of the culture to mean that he was about to do something. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Now I am about to make you a terror]

4.q: הִנְ⁠נִי֩ נֹתֶנְ⁠ךָ֨ לְ⁠מָג֜וֹר לְ⁠ךָ֣ וּ⁠לְ⁠כָל אֹהֲבֶ֗י⁠ךָ
4.note: Yahweh is speaking of Pashhur as if he would himself be **a terror** to himself and to the people close to him. He means that Pashhur will be the cause of terrible things happening to them. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Behold, I am making you the cause of terrible things happening to yourself and to all your lovers]

4.q: הִנְ⁠נִי֩ נֹתֶנְ⁠ךָ֨ לְ⁠מָג֜וֹר לְ⁠ךָ֣ וּ⁠לְ⁠כָל אֹהֲבֶ֗י⁠ךָ
4.note: The word **you** is singular here because it refers to Pashhur. So use the singular form in your translation if your language marks that distinction.
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **terror**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [into someone terrifying you and your lovers]

Yahweh is using **your lovers** as a common expression of the culture to mean “those who are your close allies.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. This also occurs in verse 6. Alternate translation: [and to all your close allies]

The pronouns **they** and **their** refer to the allies of Pashhur, not to Pashhur himself. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [and your lovers will fall by the sword of their enemies]

Here, **fall by the sword** represents die in battle. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [and their enemies will kill them in battle]

The implication is that Pashhur will watch while his allies are killed. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [and you will watch it happen with your own eyes]

Here, **the hand** represents the power and control of a person. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [into the power of the king of Babylon]
See how you translated the similar expression in 18:21.

5.note: The pronoun **they** refers to the enemies of the people of Judah, while the pronoun **them** refers to the wealth and treasures of the city. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [and their enemies will plunder these riches and take them and bring them to Babylon]

6.note: If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **captivity**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [will be taken away as captives]

The expression **you will be buried** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and there they will bury you]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **falsehood**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [you prophesied falsely]

7.note: These two clauses mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine them and express the emphasis in another way. Alternate translation: [You completely overcame my resistance, Yahweh, and I could not hold out against you]

The word translated as **persuaded** has a wide range of meaning in the original language. This could mean: (1) that Yahweh convinced Jeremiah to become his prophet. Alternate translation: [You convinced me, Yahweh, and I was convinced] (2) that Yahweh deceived Jeremiah about what serving as his prophet would involve. Alternate translation: [You misled me, Yahweh, and I was misled]

This is the beginning of what Jeremiah said to Yahweh. The text does not indicate explicitly that the speaker has changed from Yahweh to Jeremiah. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could mark that this is a direct quote of Jeremiah.

The expression **I was persuaded** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [You succeeded in persuading me]

Jeremiah is speaking of Yahweh’s call as if it were a physical struggle in which Yahweh **overpowered** him and **prevailed**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [You were too strong for me to resist, and you got your way]

Jeremiah is speaking of himself as if he were **a laughingstock**, an object of derision. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [People make fun of me]

Jeremiah is using **all the day** as a common expression of the culture to mean “continually.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. This also occurs in verse 8. Alternate translation: [continually]

Jeremiah says **everyone** as an extreme statement for emphasis. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a different way to express the emphasis. Alternate translation: [it seems that everybody is mocking me]

8.note: If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **Violence** and **destruction**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [People are acting violently and destroying things]
See how you translated **the word of Yahweh** in 8:9.

If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **reproach** and **derision**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [something that causes people to reproach and ridicule me]

The terms **reproach** and **derision** mean similar things. Jeremiah is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [a cause for utter scorn]

9.q: לֹֽא אֶזְכְּרֶ֗⁠נּוּ וְ⁠לֹֽא אֲדַבֵּ֥ר עוֹד֙ בִּ⁠שְׁמ֔⁠וֹ
9.note: The pronouns **him** and **his** refer to Yahweh. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [I will not remember Yahweh, and I will not speak again in Yahweh’s name]

Jeremiah is using **remember** as a common expression of the culture to mean “mention.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I will not mention him]

This is a double negative, consisting of the negative particle **not** and the negative word **forget**. If it would be clearer in your language, you could use a positive expression to translate this. Alternate translation: [I will forget him]

Here, **his name** represents his authority. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [and I will not speak again by his authority]

Jeremiah uses the word **But** here to indicate a contrast between his resolve to stop speaking in Yahweh’s name and his inability to hold back the message that burned within him like a fire. In your translation, indicate this contrast in a way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [Yet]
The pronoun **it** refers to the message that Yahweh had given Jeremiah to speak. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [But his message was in my heart]

Jeremiah is speaking of his inner self as if it were his **heart**, the place where his thoughts and desires exist. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [But it was within my inner being]

The point of this comparison is that just as **a burning fire** that is contained cannot be kept from breaking out, so Yahweh’s message could not be kept from being spoken. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [like a burning fire shut up in my bones that had to break out and could not be held in]

The expression **shut up** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [confining itself within my bones]

9.q: וְ⁠הָיָ֤ה בְ⁠לִבִּ⁠י֙ כְּ⁠אֵ֣שׁ בֹּעֶ֔רֶת עָצֻ֖ר בְּ⁠עַצְמֹתָ֑⁠י
9.note: Jeremiah is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [But his message was in my heart like a burning fire shut up in my bones]

10.note: See how you translated the similar expression in 6:25.

Jeremiah is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [Every man of my peace, the watchers of my stumbling, are saying]

Jeremiah is using **Every man of my peace** as a common expression of the culture to mean “everyone who was my close friend.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [All my close friends, say]

Jeremiah is speaking of his ruination as if it were a **stumbling**, a misstep that would make him fall down. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the ones watching for my ruin]

The expression **he will be deceived** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [Perhaps we can deceive him]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **vengeance**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [and we will pay him back for what he has done]

11.q: וַֽ⁠יהוָ֤ה אוֹתִ⁠י֙ כְּ⁠גִבּ֣וֹר עָרִ֔יץ עַל־כֵּ֛ן רֹדְפַ֥⁠י יִכָּשְׁל֖וּ וְ⁠לֹ֣א יֻכָ֑לוּ
11.note: The term translated as **therefore** indicates that what follows is a result of what came before. Use a connector in your language that makes this clear. Alternate translation: [But Yahweh is with me like a ruthless, mighty warrior. That is why my pursuers will stumble and will not prevail]

The point of this comparison is that just as **a ruthless mighty warrior** is able to defeat anyone who opposes him, so Yahweh is able to defeat those who oppose Jeremiah. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [But Yahweh is with me and is able to defeat my enemies, just as a ruthless, mighty warrior defeats anyone who opposes him]

Jeremiah is speaking of the failure of his enemies as if they would **stumble** while they were walking. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [my pursuers will fail and will not prevail]

The expression **will not be forgotten** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [people will never forget their everlasting humiliation]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **humiliation**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the fact that they were disgraced forever]

This is a double negative, consisting of the negative particle **not** and the negative word **forgotten**. If it would be clearer in your language, you could use a positive expression to translate this. Alternate translation: [everyone will always remember their everlasting humiliation]

12.q: וַ⁠יהוָ֤ה צְבָאוֹת֙ בֹּחֵ֣ן צַדִּ֔יק רֹאֶ֥ה כְלָי֖וֹת וָ⁠לֵ֑ב
12.note: Even though Jeremiah is addressing Yahweh directly, he is speaking of him in the third person as **Yahweh of Armies, the one testing the righteous, seeing the kidneys and the heart** to show respect. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate this in a respectful form in the second person. Alternate translation: [But you, O Yahweh of Armies, you test the righteous, you see the kidneys and the heart]
The expression **Yahweh of Armies** is a title for God. Yahweh is his name, and the title describes him as the commander of the armies of heaven.

Jeremiah is using the adjective **righteous** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [the righteous person]

Here, **the kidneys and the heart** represent “the deepest motives and thoughts of a person.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [seeing the deepest motives and thoughts of a person]

Jeremiah is speaking of his complaint as if it were a legal **cause** that he had brought before Yahweh as a judge in a court of law. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [to you I have explained what they have done to me]
See how you translated the similar expression in 11:20.

13.note: Jeremiah is using the adjective **needy** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [the person who is in need]

14.q: אָר֣וּר הַ⁠יּ֔וֹם אֲשֶׁ֥ר יֻלַּ֖דְתִּי בּ֑⁠וֹ י֛וֹם אֲשֶׁר־יְלָדַ֥תְ⁠נִי אִמִּ֖⁠י אַל־יְהִ֥י בָרֽוּךְ
14.note: These two clauses mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine them and express the emphasis in another way. Alternate translation: [I curse the day on which I was born, the day that my mother bore me]

Jeremiah is speaking of **the day on which I was born** as if it were a living thing that could receive a curse. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [May nothing good ever be said about the day on which I was born]

The expression **Cursed** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [May everyone curse the day]

The expression **I was born** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [on which my mother gave birth to me]

The expression **be blessed** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [may no one ever pronounce a blessing on it]

Jeremiah is expressing a strong meaning by using a negative word, **not**, together with a term that is the opposite of his intended meaning, **blessed**. If it would be clearer in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [let it be cursed]

15.note: See how you translated this phrase in 11:3.

The expression **has been born** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [Your wife has borne you a male child]

The pronoun **he** refers to the man who brought the news, while the pronoun **him** refers to Jeremiah’s father. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [and that man made my father very glad]

Jeremiah is repeating forms of the verb translated as **making glad** and **made him glad** in order to intensify his expression of the idea that it conveys. If your language can repeat words for intensification, it would be appropriate to do that here in your translation. If not, your language may have another way of expressing the intensification. Alternate translation: [greatly gladdening him]

16.q: וְ⁠הָיָה֙ הָ⁠אִ֣ישׁ הַ⁠ה֔וּא כֶּֽ⁠עָרִ֛ים אֲשֶׁר הָפַ֥ךְ יְהוָ֖ה וְ⁠לֹ֣א נִחָ֑ם
16.note: The point of this comparison is that just as **the cities that Yahweh overthrew** were completely destroyed, so Jeremiah wants that man to be completely destroyed. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [And let that man be completely destroyed, just as Yahweh, without relenting, completely destroyed those cities]

16.q: כֶּֽ⁠עָרִ֛ים אֲשֶׁר הָפַ֥ךְ יְהוָ֖ה וְ⁠לֹ֣א נִחָ֑ם
16.note: The implication is that **the cities** are Sodom and Gomorrah, which Yahweh destroyed completely. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [be like the cities of Sodom and Gomorrah, which Yahweh overthrew without showing them any mercy]

This is a double negative, consisting of the negative particle **not** and the negative word **relent**. If it would be clearer in your language, you could use a positive expression to translate this. Alternate translation: [and destroyed completely]

The implication is that **an outcry in the morning and a shout at the time of noon** are the sounds that people make when enemy soldiers are attacking their city. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [an outcry of people under attack in the morning and the war shout of enemy soldiers at the time of noon]

Jeremiah is saying what he wants that man to do. See the discussion in the introduction to this book about “let” and “may” and follow the decision of your team of how a speaker will express in this context what he wants someone to do. Alternate translation: [I desire that he hear an outcry] or [And he should hear an outcry]

17.note: The pronoun **he** could refer to: (1) the man who brought the news to Jeremiah’s father, whom Jeremiah has just cursed. Alternate translation: [because that man did not put me to death from the womb] (2) Yahweh, who did not allow Jeremiah to die before he was born. Alternate translation: [because Yahweh did not put me to death from the womb]
Here, **the womb** represents the time of his birth. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [when I was born]

17.q: וַ⁠תְּהִי לִ֤⁠י אִמִּ⁠י֙ קִבְרִ֔⁠י וְ⁠רַחְמָ֖⁠הֿ הֲרַ֥ת עוֹלָֽם
17.note: Jeremiah is speaking of his mother’s body as if it were **my grave**, the place where his body would remain. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [so that my body would have remained inside my mother and her womb would have stayed pregnant forever]

18.q: לָ֤⁠מָּה זֶּה֙ מֵ⁠רֶ֣חֶם יָצָ֔אתִי לִ⁠רְא֥וֹת עָמָ֖ל וְ⁠יָג֑וֹן וַ⁠יִּכְל֥וּ בְּ⁠בֹ֖שֶׁת יָמָֽ⁠י
18.note: Jeremiah is using the question form to express his anguish about having been born. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [It is dreadful that I came out from the womb only to see trouble and sorrow, and that my days come to an end in shame]

If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **trouble** and **sorrow**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [to experience troubling and sorrowful things]

Jeremiah is using **see** as a common expression of the culture to mean “experience.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [to experience trouble and sorrow]

Here, **my days** represents the years of my life. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [and the years of my life end in shame]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **shame**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [and I come to a shameful end]
